Nvidia has asked its manufacturing partners to pause shipments of AI server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to reports on 26 November 2026.
The pause applies to orders from partners such as Dell and Super Micro and is described as an unspecified period while export compliance is reviewed.
The move follows recent U.S. Commerce Department actions to close a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely from data centres in those countries.
The pause was communicated to partners after the Financial Times noted that Chinese AI labs had been renting cloud compute in the four countries to bypass U.S. export rules.

The Federal Communications Commission gave conditional approval for SpaceX to launch up to 1 million AI chip‑equipped satellites as part of its Starmind initiative.
The agency requires the first satellite to be in orbit by November 2033 and the full constellation by 2040.
The approval follows objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society, which raised concerns about debris and interference.
SpaceX describes Starmind as a solar‑powered orbital data center that will transmit data to Earth via high‑speed lasers linked to Starlink.
The company plans to manufacture the satellite chips at a new Terafab facility.
Critics, including astrophysicist Adam Becker, argue the concept is unrealistic because cooling and energy needs may still be significant.
The FCC dismissed some concerns, stating they fall outside its regulatory authority.
Putting AI compute in space aims to reduce the energy and water consumption of ground data centers.
Several firms, such as Google’s Project Suncatcher and Blue Origin’s planned launch in 2029, are exploring similar concepts.
The FCC’s sign‑off marks the first regulatory green light for a full AI satellite constellation, though opponents warn of orbital congestion and environmental risks.

Meta declined the UK Financial Conduct Authority's request to jointly test its Muse assistant in the regulator's sandbox last week, according to FCA head of innovation Colin Payne.
The FCA wants to see how the tool interacts with consumers and how payments are handled by agents such as Muse.
Payne said the regulator hopes to understand potential risks for users with low AI literacy.
problems: model check: Source mentions concern, not that the regulator hopes to understand risks.

entries.text: Payne explained the FCA is working with other UK watchdogs and has been observing AI shopping assistants from firms like Amazon.
He noted that retailers including Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, Ocado, Debenhams Group and Currys have been cooperating with Meta to enable Muse access to their sites.
The FCA is concerned that autonomous agents could prompt unintended actions, especially if consumers do not understand how the AI works, and wants safeguards to protect consumer interests.
Meta spokesperson Matthew Pollard said the company has engaged constructively with regulators and will continue to do so.
Muse, marketed as a personal assistant, launched in September and already has over 10 million users in North America.
British regulators expect similar uptake in the UK because many users already use Meta platforms like Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
The Information Commissioner’s Office emphasized the need for users to control how Muse uses personal data, adding to the regulatory focus on AI transparency.

Professor Suvrat Raju at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem he had already solved but not published, using it as a test of AI capability in theoretical physics.
He then organized a private benchmark, TheoPhysEval, by collecting unpublished problems from other physicists that typically take a day for top researchers to solve.
The benchmark was run as AI models improved, culminating in results presented at a September colloquium.
The initial test showed the AI model answered the test problem incorrectly but better than expected, prompting a formal benchmark effort.

When the full set of 50 problems was evaluated, GPT‑6 Astra solved nearly 90 % of them, correctly answering 49 of 50, and even identified errors in the human‑written solutions for the remaining cases.
Each correct answer required less than $3 of compute, comparable to the cost of a coffee in Paris, and was generated after a single human prompt.
Large language models are trained on internet text, so they may have memorized solutions to publicly discussed problems, making unseen, private problems a stricter test of genuine reasoning ability.
TheoPhysEval was designed to avoid this by using problems that had never appeared online, ensuring the AI had to reason rather than recall.
The rapid saturation of the benchmark highlights how quickly AI can reach high performance on specialized scientific tasks.
